opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't hold it against the reviewers. Looking back, I can understand where they were coming from. If you read DiT on the surface, what did we do? We took a Transformer, a standard ViT-style architecture, and replaced the U-Net backbone in a diffusion model. There's no fancy new module and no complicated new loss. To a reviewer who's used to judging papers by how many new components you invent, it can look like "you just swapped one thing for another." So "lacks novelty" is a very natural reaction.

But I think this touches on a deeper question in our field: what counts as novelty? For me, the value of DiT was never in some clever trick. It was in showing something simple and, in a way, important: the U-Net inductive bias that everyone assumed was essential for diffusion isn't actually necessary, and once you move to a Transformer you get very clean scaling behavior. More compute, more parameters, and the quality improves in a predictable way. That's an empirical insight, a kind of "removing" rather than "adding." Those kinds of contributions are often the hardest to get through peer review, because the simpler the result looks, the more people feel it was obvious.

There's actually a bit of a paradox here. In hindsight, many ideas that end up being influential look trivial. Residual connections look trivial. Scaling up a Transformer looks trivial. But before someone does it carefully and shows it works, it's not obvious at all, and most people are still putting their effort into designing more complex structures.

So I took the rejection fairly calmly. We revised it, it got into ICCV later, and over time the community, and then industry, started building on it. I think that's the right way to see peer review: it's a noisy signal over a short time window. The real test is whether people still use your work two or three years later. If I have one takeaway for students, it's this: don't pursue complexity just to look novel. If you believe something simple is true and important, do the experiments rigorously, and let time do the judging.

r001.rationale: The response explains that DiT replaced the U-Net backbone with a standard Transformer and added no new module or loss, making it look like a simple swap to reviewers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the reviewers weren't wrong on the surface, and that's what makes it interesting. If you look at the DiT paper line by line, there's no single component in there that didn't exist before. Transformers existed. Latent diffusion existed. Adaptive layer norm existed. We took these pieces, put them together very carefully, and showed that they scale. So if your definition of novelty is "a new architectural trick that nobody has seen," then yes, the paper has very little of that.

But I think that definition of novelty is a bit of a trap for the field. At the time, the dominant belief was that the U-Net inductive bias was essential for diffusion models. People had tried transformers for image generation before and gotten mediocre results, so there was this folk wisdom that convolutions were somehow necessary for the denoising task. What we wanted to do was not invent something clever, but to remove something. To strip away the U-Net and ask, very cleanly, whether the inductive bias actually mattered, or whether what mattered was compute and scale. The answer turned out to be the latter, and the scaling curves were really the whole paper. The forward FLOPs versus FID plot is the contribution, not any particular equation.

So when the paper got rejected the first time, I was frustrated, of course. Bill Peebles did an incredible job on the experiments, and we felt the result was quite clear. But I also understood it. Reviewers are trained to look for the delta, the thing you added. Simplicity is very hard to review because the delta looks like nothing. You have to read the paper and understand what belief it's refuting, and that requires context that a reviewer on a deadline may not have.

What I've come to feel is that there's a certain kind of research where the value is in the subtraction, in showing that a complicated thing can be replaced by a simple thing with no loss. That kind of work almost always looks incremental when it comes out and almost always looks obvious in retrospect. ResNeXt had a bit of that too. And I'd rather do that kind of work than add one more module to a diagram. If the field later builds on it, that's the real review process. The conference review is just the first draft of history.

r001.rationale: The candidate says DiT’s simplicity made its contribution look like “nothing” to reviewers seeking a new component, explaining the judgment that it lacked novelty.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a fair question. If you look at the ingredients separately—a diffusion model and a transformer—you can say, “Neither of these is new.” But I don’t think the value of research is only in whether every component is new. It can also be in asking whether a simple change gives us a better foundation, and then doing the experiments to understand why.

For me, the interesting question with DiT was whether transformers could be an effective, scalable backbone for diffusion models. Simply putting the two together wouldn’t be enough; the evidence matters. Does it work well? How does it behave as you scale it?

So I understand that reaction, even if I think it’s a narrow way to judge the contribution. Simplicity can make an idea look obvious once you’ve seen it. The challenge is demonstrating that the simple idea is actually useful.

r001.rationale: The response explains that the design combines familiar components and that the simple idea can look obvious, linking the novelty criticism to its simplicity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a fair question. If you describe DiT as replacing the U-Net in a diffusion model with a Transformer, it sounds very straightforward. And we weren’t inventing either Transformers or diffusion models.

But I don’t think the value of a research contribution is only in how complicated or surprising the architecture looks. There’s also value in asking whether a simple design works, testing it carefully, and understanding what happens as you scale it. That was the question we wanted to explore.

So I can understand the novelty criticism while still believing the work was worth doing. Ideally, the discussion should be about what the experiments establish and what researchers can build on from there.

r001.rationale: The response says that describing DiT as replacing a diffusion model’s U-Net with a Transformer makes it sound straightforward, then says it understands the novelty criticism.
